Steven Pinker. A Canadian-American cognitive psychologist and linguist who has brought generative grammar and cognitive science to popular audiences while contributing to debates about language acquisition, language evolution, and human nature. He developed the theory that children acquire language through an innate language instinct, drawing on Chomskyan universal grammar but grounding it in evolutionary psychology and cognitive development. He demonstrated that grammatical errors children make—saying goed or two mouses—reflect the operation of learned rules, not mere imitation, thereby supporting nativist theories of language acquisition. He argued that language is a biological adaptation shaped by natural selection, and that while its evolutionary origins remain mysterious, they deserve serious investigation. Pinker authored bestselling books including The Language Instinct and How the Mind Works, which popularised cognitive science and linguistics for general readers, making him a prominent public intellectual. His work engages not only linguistics but also evolutionary biology, psychology, philosophy of mind, and cultural criticism, attempting to synthesise insights across these disciplines. Through his writing and research, he has shown that understanding language requires understanding our evolutionary history, our cognitive development, and the embodied nature of human thought.
